\begin{abstract}
Blockchain access control for Internet of Things systems is commonly
evaluated through short laboratory tests of aggregate throughput and
latency, providing limited evidence about long-term operation and failure
behaviour. We report a \DeployDays-day Hyperledger Fabric~2.5 deployment
of hierarchical role-based access control on a 2\,ha farm in Sfax, Tunisia
(\DeploySensors{} sensors, \DeployGateways{} gateways, \DeployZones{}
zones and \TotalDecisions{} authorization decisions), followed by
controlled peer-scaling and throughput experiments. An
authorization-associated chaincode span averaged \PartAccess\,ms within
the \PartTotal\,ms write path. Across \PartRunsPerConfig{}
counterbalanced runs, increasing configured logical peers from
\ScaleMinPeers{} to \ScaleMaxPeers{} on four fixed hosts was associated
with a \PartEndorser\,ms reduction in the uninstrumented remainder. An
interleaved concurrency benchmark found that the access-control-enabled
path averaged \OverheadMeanPct\% lower throughput than the comparison
path, with no detected condition-by-concurrency interaction.

A subsequent implementation audit identified four defects that the
performance measurements did not expose: unintended role inheritance,
invalid two-residue reconstruction, inconsistent signature messages with
fail-open handling, and an on-ledger certificate-revocation check without a
functioning state-update transaction. Corrected artifacts and regression
tests are released separately from the historical implementation. A
five-run mock-stub benchmark did not detect a chaincode-execution
difference at this sample size. It does not establish equivalence or
live-network performance. The
field and network campaigns were not repeated with the corrections.
Released traces, schedules and analysis code support reproduction of the
reported historical results.
\end{abstract}

\begin{keywords}
Hierarchical role-based access control \sep Hyperledger Fabric \sep
Agricultural IoT \sep Edge computing \sep Performance measurement \sep
Certificate revocation \sep Reproducible research
\end{keywords}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}
%%============================================================================

A precision farm is a multi-stakeholder system before it is a technical one.
Soil probes, weather stations and irrigation actuators produce readings
continuously \cite{zhang2002precision}, and the people who consume those
readings want different and partly conflicting things from them: farmers
need operational control, agronomists need history but no actuation rights,
certification bodies need compliance evidence without visibility into
commercially sensitive agronomic detail, supply-chain partners need
provenance but not real-time operations, and regulators need environmental
records.

Handing this authorization matrix to a single server concentrates the risk
in one place. An attacker who takes that server gains not only the data but,
on a farm with networked valves, the irrigation itself
\cite{benedict2021decentralized}, and the audit log that would reconstruct
the incident is written by the machine that was compromised. Surveying
agricultural IoT deployments, Ferrag et al.\ \cite{ferrag2020security} found
most lacked fine-grained access control at all, and Kamilaris et
al.\ \cite{kamilaris2019rise} and recent convergence surveys
\cite{rustemi2025synergizing} find blockchain work in agriculture
concentrated almost entirely on post-harvest supply-chain tracking rather
than pre-harvest authorization. Recording role assignments, revocations
and access decisions on a permissioned ledger can reduce dependence on a
single policy database and make authorized changes auditable across
participating organizations; it does not eliminate trust in the
certificate authority, administrators, gateway software, endorsement
configuration or chaincode implementation. What is unsettled is the
cost of the part it does change, and specifically where that cost falls.

\subsection{Problem statement}
\label{subsec:problem}

Existing blockchain access-control studies for IoT mainly report short
laboratory measurements of end-to-end latency and throughput. These
measurements do not show whether authorization dominates transaction delay,
whether results persist during long deployments, or whether the implemented
policy matches its specification. Agricultural deployments add constrained
devices, intermittent connectivity, low-rate radio links, and certificate
lifecycle events that short benchmarks rarely exercise
\cite{abang2024latency,ferrag2020security,rustemi2025synergizing}.

This study addresses that evidence gap through a field deployment, controlled
configuration experiments, and an implementation audit. The available timing
field does not isolate every Fabric stage, so it is reported only as an
authorization-associated span. This distinction prevents unsupported
attribution while retaining the measured comparison.

These questions structure the rest of the paper:

\begin{description}
\item[RQ1] What latency and throughput differences are observed between the
  tested access-control-enabled configuration and the access-control-free
  comparison configuration?
\item[RQ2] How is configured logical peer count associated with
  client-observed write latency under the deployed topology?
\item[RQ3] Which implementation and observability failures survived the
  field deployment, and why did the existing tests not detect them?
\end{description}

The contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
\item a \DeployDays{}-day field evaluation covering \TotalDecisions{}
authorization decisions across \DeploySensors{} sensors and
\DeployGateways{} gateways;
\item controlled run-level analyses of write latency, logical peer
multiplicity, and access-control throughput;
\item an implementation audit identifying policy, residue-recovery,
signature-verification and certificate-revocation defects, plus a
revocation-observability gap now partly closed in code; and
\item a reproducible artifact containing data, code, schedules, tests, and
analysis outputs.
\end{itemize}

Section~\ref{sec:related} positions the work. Section~\ref{sec:design}
presents the system design, Section~\ref{sec:impl} describes the
implementation, Section~\ref{sec:method} explains the methodology,
Section~\ref{sec:results} reports the results, Section~\ref{sec:discussion}
discusses their implications, and Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes.

%%============================================================================
\section{Related work}
\label{sec:related}
%%============================================================================

\subsection{Access control for constrained devices}
\label{subsec:rw_models}

Role-based access control as formalised by Sandhu et al.\ \cite{sandhu1996role}
and standardised by NIST \cite{ferraiolo2001role} is still the reference
model for multi-stakeholder authorization, and its IoT adaptations share a
structural assumption that becomes awkward in the field: some trusted
decision component must be reachable when access is requested. RBAC
extensions for IoT \cite{ye2015iot}, attribute-based evaluation
\cite{hu2014guide,servos2017abac,sciancalepore2017oauth} and capability-token
delegation \cite{hernandez2017capability} place that trust in a policy
engine, an attribute authority and a credential issuer respectively,
retaining a central enforcement point \cite{ye2015iot,servos2017abac},
distributing revocation into tokens rather than solving it
\cite{hernandez2017capability}, or splitting the model between humans and
devices while leaving the role store centralised
\cite{alshehri2016access}. Sciancalepore et
al.\ \cite{sciancalepore2017oauth} quantify what open-standard authorization
stacks cost on constrained hardware, the empirical case for moving policy
evaluation off the sensor entirely; Novo \cite{novo2018blockchain} argued
early that the role store itself belongs on a distributed ledger. We take
that as given and ask what it costs.

\subsection{Blockchain-based access control and how it is evaluated}
\label{subsec:rw_blockchain}

Capability-token systems on public chains established feasibility without
practicality: FairAccess \cite{ouaddah2016fairaccess} encodes grants as
Bitcoin-like transfers with confirmation windows measured in minutes, and
BlendCAC \cite{xu2018blendcac} uses ERC-721 tokens with per-transaction fees
no sensor duty cycle can absorb. Neither addresses role hierarchy,
geographic scoping or seasonal expiry, which agriculture actually needs.

Permissioned platforms remove the latency and fee obstacles, and Fabric-based
IoT work has grown accordingly: testbed architectures and performance models
\cite{shih2022iiot,pajooh2022fabric_iot,kepark2023fabric_model}, trust and
reputation layers \cite{putra2021trust}, contract-enforced domain policy on
cloud-hosted nodes where memory and thermal limits do not apply
\cite{usman2024blockchain}, and a data marketplace at scale
\cite{gonzalez2023marketplace}. All report aggregate throughput and latency
from a controlled setting. Two are closer to our method: Idrissi and
Palmieri \cite{idrissi2024blockchain_jsupercomput} give an end-to-end Fabric
latency breakdown on constrained ARM hardware in a healthcare context, the
nearest methodological precedent for the partition in
Section~\ref{subsubsec:partition}, and Tzenetopoulos et
al.\ \cite{tzenetopoulos2022hlfkubed} establish a Raspberry Pi 3B+ reference
point discussed in Section~\ref{sec:discussion}.

Table~\ref{tab:related} summarises how these and further systems
\cite{zaidi2023fabrication,bandara2021modeling} are evaluated: laboratory
testbeds or simulation, runs of hours or days, aggregate reporting. We have
not found prior work that times an authorization-associated span separately
from the rest of the write path on a field deployment this long, or that
reports revocation behaviour over a multi-week window. That combination is
the contribution, not any single mechanism in Section~\ref{sec:design} and
not a validated stage-by-stage decomposition.

\subsection{Agricultural IoT and edge infrastructure}
\label{subsec:rw_agri}

Blockchain in agriculture has concentrated on traceability after harvest
\cite{tian2017traceability,lin2018blockchain,bandara2021modeling}, where the
unit of interest is a shipment rather than a zone-scoped actuation. Safeer et
al.\ \cite{safeer2025agrifarming} combine computer vision, IoT and blockchain
for climate-smart cultivation and, like most pre-harvest work, treat
authorization as an implementation detail rather than a measured component.
Liu et al.\ \cite{liu2019edge} and Wang et al.\ \cite{wang2021edge} reduce
processing latency at the agricultural edge without addressing the
authorization layer above it, and Mohanta et al.\ \cite{mohanta2025smartgrid}
apply smart-contract enforcement in smart grids, a neighbouring domain with
comparable device constraints and a similarly centralised starting point.

On identity infrastructure, W3C Decentralized Identifiers
\cite{w3c_did_core} and gateway-assisted verification for constrained devices
\cite{ferdous2019ssi,tara2023decentralized} offer an eventual migration away
from X.509, treated here as future work rather than a deployed alternative.
On the radio side, Adelantado et al.\ \cite{adelantado2017understanding}
characterise the LoRaWAN capacity limits that bound achievable sensor density
per gateway, a constraint visible in the energy results (Supplement~S6).

%%============================================================================
\section{Access-control design}
\label{sec:design}
%%============================================================================

\subsection{Deployment structure and threat model}
\label{subsec:threat}

The deployment has three tiers, shown in Figure~\ref{fig:architecture}.
ESP32-WROOM-32 sensor nodes (dual-core Xtensa LX6 at 240\,MHz, 520\,kB SRAM)
sample soil and environmental data, sign each reading with an Ed25519 key
held in one-time-programmable eFuse, and transmit over LoRa. Raspberry Pi~4B
zone gateways (quad-core Cortex-A72, 4\,GB LPDDR4, TPM~2.0) receive those
payloads, verify signatures, endorse Fabric transactions and cache policy
decisions locally. A Fabric network of four peers, one per zone, three Raft
orderers and CouchDB~3.2 for world state maintains the ledger. Gateways
interconnect over a BATMAN-adv mesh \cite{batman2010} that reroutes around
individual gateway failures and carries Fabric gossip and certificate
revocation list (CRL) traffic between zones.

Following the permissioned-blockchain model in which every participant is
credentialed \cite{androulaki2018fabric}, orderers and the certificate
authority are operated by vetted institutional entities and treated as
non-malicious; Raft's $2f+1$ crash-fault tolerance \cite{ongaro2014raft}
means the three-node cluster survives one orderer failure but not a
reachable orderer behaving maliciously, a boundary Byzantine-tolerant
ordering \cite{yin2019hotstuff,castro1999practical,hyperledger2025whatsnew}
would widen at higher consensus cost. Sensors, client devices and every
wireless channel are treated as potentially compromised; physical
tampering and side-channel extraction against cryptographic accelerators
sit outside the evaluated scope (Section~\ref{sec:discussion}).

The design and the evaluation below distinguish six properties:
\emph{authentication}, \emph{authorization}, \emph{integrity},
\emph{freshness}, \emph{auditability} and \emph{availability}. The
deployment gives usable evidence about authorization
(Section~\ref{subsec:security}), auditability (every decision writes an
audit entry, Section~\ref{subsec:chaincode}) and availability
(Section~\ref{subsec:availability}); it does not give usable evidence about
authentication or integrity of sensor readings, because the signature path
meant to bind a reading to its sensor did not function
(Section~\ref{subsec:pm_signature}), and freshness is architectural (nonce
checking) rather than measured against an adaptive adversary.

\subsection{Role hierarchy}
\label{subsec:roles}

Following the treatment of hierarchical role administration in ARBAC97
\cite{sandhu1999arbac97}, a partial order $\preceq$ over the role set $R$
defines inheritance, with $r_i \preceq r_j$ iff
$\mathrm{perm}(r_i) \subseteq \mathrm{perm}(r_j)$. The deployed hierarchy
(Figure~\ref{fig:hierarchy}) is a human chain and a separate device chain,
both below Admin:
\begin{align}
\mathrm{SupplyChain} \preceq \mathrm{Certifier}
  &\preceq \mathrm{Agronomist} \notag\\
  &\preceq \mathrm{Farmer} \preceq \mathrm{Admin}
  \label{eq:human}\\
\mathrm{Sensor} &\preceq \mathrm{Gateway} \preceq \mathrm{Admin}
  \label{eq:device}
\end{align}

Separating auditors from operational staff is the requirement that motivated
the model: an auditor should read compliance evidence without inheriting the
agronomic permissions a farm treats as proprietary. Placing Certifier inside
the human chain rather than beside it defeats that: Agronomist and Farmer
inherit Certifier's permissions, including \texttt{ReadAudit}, so the
deployment did \emph{not} confine audit-log access to auditors. We did not
intend this and did not notice it until the implementation was audited
against the manuscript for this article. We report the model as deployed,
because that is the model the measurements describe; Table~\ref{tab:permdiff}
gives the rows where intended, deployed and corrected policy disagree, and
Section~\ref{subsec:pm_policy} the full account.

\end{tikzpicture}
\caption{Seven-role hierarchy implemented in the deployed chaincode.}
\label{fig:hierarchy}
\end{figure}

The effective permission set of user $u$ in a session is
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{eff}(u) = \bigcup_{r \in \mathrm{active}(u)}
  \; \bigcup_{r' \preceq r} pa(r'),
\end{equation}
where $pa(r)$ are the permissions assigned directly to $r$ and
$\mathrm{active}(u)$ the non-expired roles held by $u$. An access request
$(u, \mathit{op}, \mathit{res}, t)$ is granted iff
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
&\exists\, r \in \mathrm{active}(u,t):
  (\mathit{op},\mathit{res}) \in \mathrm{eff}(r)\\
&\quad \land\;
  \bigl(\mathrm{zone}(u) = \mathrm{zone}(\mathit{res})
  \;\lor\; \mathrm{czt}(u, \mathrm{zone}(\mathit{res}), t)\bigr),
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:grant}
\end{equation}
where $\mathrm{czt}(u,z,t)$ holds iff $u$ has a valid administrator-issued
cross-zone token for $z$ at time $t$, and
$\mathrm{active}(u,t) = \{r \mid \exists\,\mathrm{assign}(u,r,t_s,t_e):
t_s \le t \le t_e\}$. The full effective-permission matrix this produces for
all seven roles, generated from \texttt{roles.go} rather than transcribed,
is Table~S2 in the supplementary material; Table~\ref{tab:permdiff} below
gives only the rows that differ between what was intended, what was
deployed, and what the released correction changes.

\label{tab:permdiff}
\footnotesize
\begin{tabularx}{\columnwidth}{@{}lXccc@{}}
\toprule
Permission & Role & Intended & Deployed & Corrected \\
\midrule
\texttt{ReadAudit}   & {\scriptsize Agronomist} & No & Yes & No \\
\texttt{ReadAudit}   & Farmer     & No & Yes & No \\
\texttt{ReadZone}    & Certifier  & No & Yes & No \\
\texttt{ControlZone} & {\scriptsize Agronomist} & No & Yes & No \\

and Farmer and \texttt{ControlZone} to Farmer; see

\end{table}

\subsection{Zone and temporal scoping}
\label{subsec:zones}

Geographic farm regions (North, South, East, West) define the zone model,
enforced at three independent points: certificate SAN field, gateway
enrollment (own zone only), and chaincode's ASN.1-decoded zone check on
every transaction, chosen over PEM-text matching because the latter is
spoofable by an attacker who controls the subject field. Cross-zone
tokens are administrator-issued and recorded immutably, so a temporary
grant expires on its own rather than needing a reissued certificate.
Temporal constraints run in two independent layers, the chaincode's
\texttt{ExpiresAt} check against the Fabric transaction timestamp and the
Fabric MSP's X.509 \texttt{NotAfter} validation, so a seasonal worker
loses access at expiry without administrator action, recorded as a new
audit entry; GPS-sourced gateway time, NTP fallback, sits comfortably
inside the $\pm$5-minute enforcement window.

The decision procedure Equation~\eqref{eq:grant} describes is given in
full as Algorithm~S4 in the supplementary material. Two of its properties
matter later. First, the work is bounded and independent of which
operation was requested (hierarchy walked to depth at most three, zone
check a single field comparison), the mechanism we would expect to produce
similar costs across operations. Second, every path, including every
denial, writes an audit entry, so \texttt{CheckAccess} is state-mutating
and commits through ordering exactly as a sensor write does, with expired
assignments revoked inside the same transaction that denies the request.

\subsection{Cascading enrollment}
\label{subsec:enrollment}

An ESP32 cannot hold the TLS handshake state that direct interaction with a
certificate authority requires (mbedTLS on ESP-IDF needs roughly 70\,kB of
heap against a 520\,kB SRAM budget \cite{raza2013lithe}), so registration
authority moves down the tier structure in three stages (Supplement,
Figure~S1 and Algorithm~S1): administrator credentials, then gateway
registration with the private key in TPM~2.0, then sensor enrollment with
the gateway as local registration authority. The sensor's key is generated
on-device and never transmitted, so compromising a gateway does not yield
it, and re-provisioning a lost key needs physical access, since eFuse
programming is irreversible: but the key is \emph{not} read-protected:
software signing copies it from eFuse into RAM each time, and setting the
read-disable bit would break signing outright on this ESP32, which has no
hardware Ed25519 engine. Read protection needs a different part (the
ESP32-S3's HMAC and digital-signature peripherals); the eFuse here gives
durability against reflashing, not extraction resistance against code
running on the device, and Section~\ref{sec:discussion} counts key
extraction by an attacker with code execution as residual risk.

\section{Implementation}
\label{sec:impl}
%%============================================================================

\subsection{Chaincode and transaction flow}
\label{subsec:chaincode}

The chaincode is written in Go~1.21 against \texttt{fabric-contract-api-go}
and targets Fabric~2.5. Eight transactions are exposed in the deployed
package: \texttt{AssignRole}, \texttt{RevokeRole}, \texttt{RenewRole},
\texttt{CheckAccess}, \texttt{IssueCrossZoneToken},
\texttt{RevokeCrossZoneToken}, \texttt{GetAuditLog} and \texttt{PruneNonces};
the corrected package adds a ninth, \texttt{UpdateCRL}, described in
Section~\ref{subsec:pm_revocation}. Figure~\ref{fig:flow} places the
access-control check inside Fabric's execute-order-validate pipeline. An
authorization denial is a successful chaincode response carrying
\textsc{Deny} plus an audit write, so a denial is ordered and committed like
any other transaction; only an endorsement-level failure stops before the
orderer reaches it.

\centering

Three implementation decisions shape the measurements. Every state-mutating
call carries a UUID nonce recorded in world state, rejected on reuse before
any state is read, which defeats replay inside the timestamp window. Every
access attempt, granted or denied, writes an audit entry holding the caller's
certificate hash, operation, resource, zone, decision and reason, so the
audit trail is a byproduct of enforcement rather than a parallel log that can
drift from it. And \texttt{CheckAccess} revokes an expired assignment in the
same transaction that denies the request, which makes even a read-intent
check state-mutating and therefore endorsed rather than served as a query.

Peer configuration for the ARM64 gateways uses 50 transactions per block, a
500\,ms batch timeout, a 256\,MB state cache, endorsement restricted to
zone-local peers, Snappy compression on LevelDB and 5-minute gRPC keepalive,
targeting the write amplification that dominates latency on microSD-backed
storage, within the parameter space Abang et al.\ \cite{abang2024latency}
identify as governing Fabric latency.

\subsection{Sensor firmware and residue-coded transmission}
\label{subsec:firmware}

The sensor certificate lives in battery-backed RTC slow memory so it
survives deep sleep, guarded by a CRC and a magic sentinel checked on each
wake; a mismatch forces re-enrollment rather than transmission under an
unverifiable identity. Signing uses wolfSSL's Ed25519 implementation: the
firmware hashes the payload with hardware SHA-256 and signs the resulting
32-byte digest, a prehash construction that is neither standard Ed25519
(which hashes the message internally with SHA-512) nor Ed25519ph (which
prehashes with SHA-512 under a distinct domain separator). Nothing in the
deployment depends on the difference, but a reimplementation from the
paper alone would not interoperate unless the prehash is reproduced. The
main loop wakes every \DutyCycleMinutes{} minutes, verifies the cached
certificate, samples the sensors, signs the payload, transmits and returns
to deep sleep.

Readings are transmitted as residues rather than plaintext values: a value
is reduced modulo the pairwise-coprime set $\{97, 101, 103\}$ and the three
residues go out as separate single-byte packets, any two of which
reconstruct the original by the Chinese Remainder Theorem
\cite{garner1959residue} (Supplement~S2). The admissible range is where
this scheme goes wrong, and the deployed firmware got it wrong: recovery
from an arbitrary \emph{pair} is unique only below the smallest pairwise
product of the moduli, not below their product (Section~\ref{subsec:pm_crt}).
The corrected firmware uses $\{253, 254, 255\}$, a pairwise bound of
$64\,262$, and quantises soil moisture from twelve to eight bits so the
packed value reaches $51\,455$ and stays inside it; keeping twelve bits
would require all three residues and forfeit the redundancy entirely.

The deployment trace does not record the regional radio band, sub-band
allocation, or gateway downlink airtime. We therefore make no claim of
regulatory duty-cycle compliance from these data. Any deployment using an
EU868 plan must verify node and gateway duty-cycle limits for its actual
sub-band, payload, retries and downlink acknowledgements; that verification
is outside the present measurement.

\subsection{Gateway services and revocation propagation}
\label{subsec:gateway}

Each gateway runs Fabric~2.5 from official ARM64 binaries. A Python
enrollment service bound to the local interface accepts CSRs only from
sensors in its own zone and rate-limits per source address, and a policy
cache with a \RevCacheTTL-second nominal TTL absorbs repeated checks from
the same sensor during a transmission burst. Revocation publication and
cache invalidation (Supplement, Algorithm~S3) is the mechanism whose
behaviour we most wanted to observe over a long window, and one branch is
the whole story of Section~\ref{subsec:revocation}: for a reachable
gateway the cache is invalidated by the CRL event itself, so staleness is
bounded by gossip propagation and the nominal TTL never binds, while for an
unreachable one the bound falls back to the scheduled refresh interval.
In the intended design, gateway reachability determines whether
event-driven invalidation is available or whether the scheduled refresh
path is required; because the historical trace lacks complete episode
identifiers and synchronised connectivity state, it cannot establish
which branch was followed in any given observed case.

\subsection{Formal specification}
\label{subsec:tla}

A three-role subset of the model is specified in TLA+ and checked with TLC
\cite{lamport2002specifying,newcombe2015amazon}, finding no violation of
the role-permission invariant under weak fairness. This is a sanity check
on a small model, not verification of the deployed framework: it covers
three of seven roles, omits zone and temporal predicates, and nothing
connects it to the Go implementation, the binding gap given that the
implemented hierarchy differs from the specified one
(Section~\ref{subsec:pm_policy}). The specification is in the artifact.

\section{Measurement methodology}
\label{sec:method}
%%============================================================================

\subsection{Site and workload}
\label{subsec:deployment}

The system was deployed for \DeployDays{} days on a 2\,ha experimental
farm near Sfax, Tunisia, from 1~August to 30~September 2025. The released
trace reports the site only at settlement level; precise field coordinates
are excluded. Ambient temperature reached 39.5\textdegree{}C, and the
deployment recorded three operational connectivity interruptions rather
than injected faults. Table~\ref{tab:deployment} gives the configuration.

Each sensor reported on a \DutyCycleMinutes-minute duty cycle, giving
\WritesPerDay{} sensor writes per day and \SensorWrites{} over the
deployment; human and administrative traffic (farmer and agronomist
queries, certifier audits, supply-chain reads, role operations) brings the
total to \TotalDecisions{} recorded authorization decisions, of which
\TotalDenied{} (\DenyRatePct\%) were ordinary-operation denials.

\label{tab:deployment}

                            (settlement-level location only) \\

\subsection{Peer-scaling topology}
\label{subsec:topology}

Section~\ref{subsec:scaling} varies \emph{configured logical peer count},
not physical capacity: increasing configured peers does not automatically
reduce Fabric latency, since the effect depends on the endorsement policy,
endorser selection, connection pooling, proposal fan-out, and peer CPU and
state-database load. Only the \ScaleMinPeers-peer configuration is the
physically deployed network of Table~\ref{tab:deployment}, one peer per
zone on its own Raspberry Pi; the \num{8}-, \num{16}- and \num{32}-peer
configurations run additional logical peers on the same four physical
hosts, oversubscribed rather than added, so the comparison isolates
endorser multiplicity under a fixed endorsement policy, not physical
capacity. The full topology and routing table (endorsement policy,
orderer topology, batch parameters, CPU/memory allocation, all identical
across configurations) is Table~S3 in the supplementary material.

A run is one workload execution at a fixed peer count. Each run contains
130 samples collected over 4~h 18~min and is followed by a 42-min gap,
forming a five-hour slot. The acquisition protocol specified peer and
orderer restarts during that gap. The CSV records the schedule but not a
reset-completion flag or retained-state measurement. We therefore use the
run as the analysis unit, adjust for recorded sequence, and do not claim
that the trace excludes all residual carry-over.

\subsection{Instrumentation}
\label{subsec:instrumentation}

Nine trace streams were recorded: per-decision records (caller identity,
role, operation, resource, zone, decision, denial reason, latency),
per-transaction sensor records (signature validity, residues received,
transmission energy), and dedicated campaigns for peer-scaling latency,
throughput, LoRa energy in single-channel and residue modes,
cryptographic timings, revocation lifecycle, authorization-boundary
attempts and outages. Latency is measured at the gateway between
submission and commit notification (endorsement through commitment,
excluding only the LoRa hop); throughput is committed transactions per
measurement window; energy uses an INA219 sensor at 2\,kHz. The baseline
for overhead attribution (Section~\ref{subsec:throughput}) is the
identical network, workload and hardware with the access-control
chaincode removed, which also removes the audit write and nonce check, so
the difference estimates the cost of the complete access-control-enabled
path, not an isolated permission decision.

\subsection{Statistical treatment}
\label{subsec:stats}

Getting the independent experimental unit wrong is the most common way a
measurement study overstates precision. Transactions generated in the same
run, day or gateway are correlated, and treating each one as an independent
replicate produces standard errors far smaller than the design actually
supports. Table~\ref{tab:units} states, for every comparison in this
article, what that unit is; the two campaigns discussed below use the run
(\PartRunsPerConfig{} per peer-count configuration and 5 per throughput
cell), not the transaction. The throughput runs belong to one session and
are not presented as independent sessions.

\begin{table}[pos=t]
\caption{Independent experimental unit used for each analysis in this article.}
\label{tab:units}
\small
\begin{tabularx}{\columnwidth}{@{}lX@{}}
\toprule
Analysis & Independent unit \\
\midrule
Throughput vs.\ concurrency &
  Run within one interleaved session (5 per cell per arm) \\
Access-control invariance across peer counts &
  Run-level observation, 8 per configuration in 8 counterbalanced blocks \\
Peer-count latency comparison &
  Run-level observation, 8 per configuration in 8 counterbalanced blocks \\
Operation-label diagnostic &
  Deployment day (\DeployDays{} days) \\
Revocation stage records &
  Reported descriptively; stages do not resolve into independent episodes \\
Security campaign &
  Executed test corpus, not a random sample of attacks; no interval given \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{table}

Group comparisons use Welch's $t$-test, reported with the mean difference,
its 95\% confidence interval and Cohen's $d$; comparisons across more than
two independent groups use one-way ANOVA. Where an order effect is a live
concern, a multiple regression on the relevant factors is used instead of a
simple group comparison, so the factor of interest and run order are
estimated jointly rather than one being assumed away by design alone
(Section~\ref{subsec:scaling}).

The released peer-scaling trace contains each configuration in the recorded
counterbalanced sequence, and the released throughput trace interleaves the
two arms within each concurrency cell. The reported observations are the
run-level records in the repository, not a reordering of values from the
field deployment and not an assumption that transaction rows are
independent. The campaign metadata are retained in the raw files and
supplementary tables: \PartRunsPerConfig{} runs per configured peer count in
counterbalanced order (Supplement, Table~S8), and the two throughput arms
interleaved within every concurrency cell. Both now support an explicit
order-effect
test: a joint regression of peer-scaling run means on $\log_2(\text{peers})$
and centred run sequence finds no sequence effect on the recorded span
($p=\OrderEffectSpanP$) or total latency ($p=\OrderEffectTotalP$) once
peer count is in the model, while the peer-count effect on total latency
remains significant at $p\OrderEffectTotalPeerP$; pooling each throughput
run's deviation from its own cell-and-arm mean against its position in the
interleaved session finds no trend ($R^2=\OrderEffectRSq$, $p=\OrderEffectP$)
. These checks reduce, but do not eliminate, concern about campaign-order
effects.

Confidence intervals on means use the Student-$t$ interval where
$n \ge 1000$ and a percentile bootstrap of 10\,000 resamples below that;
the peer-scaling P95 interval resamples whole runs rather than individual
transactions, and the ten throughput comparisons are corrected for
multiplicity with Holm-Bonferroni (\OverheadHolmSig{} of \OverheadLevels{}
remain significant after adjustment). We deliberately attach no interval
to the security block rate or the revocation stage records, since
repetitions of a scripted scenario and correlated stages of one episode
are not independent samples. Equivalence claims use two one-sided tests
against a $\pm$\DecisionMargin\,ms margin fixed after the data were
already available to us, not preregistered, and reported as such; that
margin is about 3.5\% of the \DecisionMean\,ms decision cost.

\subsection{Reproducibility}
\label{subsec:repro}

Every number, table and figure in this article is generated from the
released traces by \texttt{analysis/derive\_results.py}, which reads the
raw traces, recomputes the statistical summary and emits both a
machine-readable results file and the LaTeX macros and table bodies this
manuscript expands; a repository test asserts that every macro matches the
corresponding derived value, so nothing measured is transcribed by hand
and the agreement is tested rather than assumed. This verifies numerical consistency with the implemented pipeline, not the scientific validity of the source data or analytical assumptions. The pipeline also emits
a SHA-256 digest, byte count and row count for each of the \TraceCount{}
input traces (\TraceRows{} rows total), and resampling uses a fixed seed.
The repository carries the historical implementation associated with the
measurements and a separate corrected package described in
Section~\ref{subsec:pm_policy}; the corrected package did not generate the
historical performance results. Readers should cite the archived research artifact and its permanent DOI. The repository build script regenerates and recompiles the manuscript and derived outputs in one command, and a data dictionary (\texttt{data/raw/README.md}) marks fields
withdrawn or reinterpreted following the implementation audit. A second driver,
\texttt{analysis/run\_campaign.py}, repeats the throughput, latency and
decision-cost campaigns against a live Fabric network in the same schema,
so an independent installation's measurements can be substituted and the
article regenerated against them; it does not reproduce the energy and
cryptographic-timing traces, which need the INA219 bench above.

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}
%%============================================================================

\subsection{Field-deployment latency accounting for the write path}
\label{subsec:decomposition}

Both transaction classes in the trace are endorsed, ordered and committed,
since as Section~\ref{subsec:chaincode} explains every authorization outcome
writes an audit entry. The interesting question is not which class is
slower but how much of a write is associated with the access-control layer,
and the chaincode logs a timing field on every write towards answering it:
\texttt{rbac\_overhead\_ms}, recorded alongside end-to-end latency.

\subsubsection{A descriptive account, not a stage decomposition}
\label{subsubsec:partition}

For each configured logical peer count, write-path latency is reported as
total latency, the recorded authorization-associated span, and what is
left once that span is subtracted (``remaining latency''), a plain
subtraction rather than a claim that the two are independently identified
Fabric stages (Scope~S1, Section~\ref{sec:discussion}).

The recorded span, averaged over the campaign, is \PartAccess\,ms; we
deliberately do not call this a direct measurement of permission-evaluation
cost, since the timing field's exact instrumentation boundaries cannot be
reconstructed from the deployed source (S1), and it is also larger than a
complete standalone \texttt{CheckAccess} transaction, \DecisionMean\,ms
(Section~\ref{subsec:byclass}), because the two counters do not share a
documented boundary. The remaining latency falls from \PartRemainder\,ms
plus \PartEndorser\,ms at \ScaleMinPeers{} peers to \PartRemainder\,ms at
\ScaleMaxPeers{} peers, a \PartEndorser\,ms reduction across the tested
range (Table~\ref{tab:partition}); nothing here identifies which of
ordering, validation, commit, or the peer-count-sensitive part of
endorsement execution accounts for it, and \PartRemainder\,ms at the
largest configuration is a baseline, not an identified floor, since the
remainder was still falling, with decrements per doubling growing rather
than shrinking, at \ScaleMaxPeers{} peers.

\input{tables/tab_partition}

\subsubsection{The recorded span is stable in configured peer count}
\label{subsubsec:acinvariance}

That the recorded span can be treated as approximately constant is tested,
not assumed. The design contains \PartRunsPerConfig{} run-level observations
per configured peer count, counterbalanced across eight blocks. Two complete
4x4 Latin squares place every configuration in each serial position twice
(Supplement, Table~S8).

Across the four configured peer counts, the per-configuration means span
\PartSpread\,ms with no monotonic trend ($\PartTrendSlope$\,ms per doubling,
$p=\PartTrendP$, $n=32$ runs). The extreme configurations
(\ScaleMinPeers{} and \ScaleMaxPeers{} peers) have a within-block mean
difference of \PartTostDiff\,ms. Its 90\% interval,
[\PartTostLow, \PartTostHigh]\,ms, is inside the exploratory
$\pm$\DecisionMargin\,ms margin (TOST $p=\PartTostP$). This margin was
selected after data inspection, so the result is not confirmatory. A joint
regression on peer count and centred run
sequence finds no sequence effect on the span once peer count is in the
model ($p=\OrderEffectSpanP$). Because the span does not
shrink when peers are added, its share of the write path \emph{rises}: from
\PartAccessPct\% at \ScaleMinPeers{} peers to \PartAccessPctAtMax\% of the
smaller total at \ScaleMaxPeers{} peers. That is the opposite of what a
designer would assume from the \ScaleMinPeers-peer figure alone.

Splitting the remaining latency into ordering, validation, commit and the
peer-count-sensitive part of endorsement needs a transaction timestamped at
each Fabric hand-off, which we did not collect (S1); read with that
boundary in mind, Table~\ref{tab:partition} answers the question a designer
actually faces, how much of the budget is associated with the
access-control layer, without claiming a stage attribution the
measurements cannot support.

\subsection{Latency by operation class}
\label{subsec:byclass}

Policy evaluations (\texttt{CheckAccess}, pooled across the \DecisionOps{}
operation types recorded) average \DecisionMean\,ms (SD \DecisionSD) and
sensor writes \WriteMean\,ms (SD \WriteSD, P95 \WritePNinetyFive, P99
\WritePNinetyNine), a \CommitCost\,ms gap between operation classes that
differ simultaneously in payload size, world-state access and endorsement
work; consensus is common to both, so this is not the cost of consensus,
and should not be confused with the write-path accounting above, which is
derived within rather than across classes (full table and CDF figure,
Supplement Table~S5 and Figure~S3). The \DecisionOps{} operation types are
pooled rather than broken out because, across the \PolicyCells{}
role-by-operation cells in the trace, the grant rate is uniformly between
\PolicyGrantMin\% and \PolicyGrantMax\%: a trace in which the recorded
operation and role determined the policy path would instead show cells
near 0\% or 100\%, so these labels do not separate policy-distinct
executions and do not support an operation- or privilege-specific
comparison. The scripted campaign in Section~\ref{subsec:security}, where
every boundary-crossing request was refused, is the evidence that the
policy itself discriminates; whether privilege level or hierarchy depth
affects decision \emph{cost} needs a designed experiment
(Section~\ref{sec:discussion}).

\subsection{Interleaved throughput experiment}
\label{subsec:throughput}

Figure~\ref{fig:throughput} reports throughput against offered concurrency
for the HRBAC configuration and the access-control-free baseline on
identical hardware and workload.

\begin{widefig}
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}
\begin{axis}[paperplot,
  width=\linewidth, height=5.0cm,
  xlabel={Offered concurrency (clients)},
  ylabel={Throughput (TPS)},
  xmin=0, xmax=110, ymin=30, ymax=80,
  legend pos=south east]
\addplot+[mark=*, mark size=1.7pt, blue!65!black,
  error bars/.cd, y dir=both, y explicit]
  table[x=clients, y=baseline, y error=baseline_sd] {figdata/throughput.dat};
\addlegendentry{Fabric without access control}
\addplot+[mark=square*, mark size=1.7pt, red!65!black,
  error bars/.cd, y dir=both, y explicit]
  table[x=clients, y=hrbac, y error=hrbac_sd] {figdata/throughput.dat};
\addlegendentry{HRBAC}
\draw[gray!70, dashed] (axis cs:\KneeClients,30) -- (axis cs:\KneeClients,80);
\node[font=\scriptsize, text=gray!55!black, anchor=south west]
  at (axis cs:\KneeClients,73) {observed peak};
\end{axis}
\end{tikzpicture}
\caption{Mean throughput and standard deviation across five interleaved runs per concurrency level.}
\label{fig:throughput}
\end{widefig}

The primary analysis is a single blocked factorial regression over every
run, with terms for condition, concurrency, their interaction, and a
position covariate, rather than ten independent per-level Welch tests. The
ten concurrency levels were tested in one fixed ascending order, not
counterbalanced across the session, so a run's raw campaign-wide sequence
number is almost collinear with its concurrency level
($r=\ThrPositionConcurrCorr$ in this dataset) and cannot serve as an
independent order covariate; only the two conditions are interleaved within
each level. The position term below is therefore each run's centred
position \emph{within its own concurrency level's 10-run cell} (five
interleaved HRBAC/baseline pairs). That construction makes it orthogonal to
concurrency, and it is where a within-session warming or ledger-growth
trend would actually show up.

The model estimates a \ThrCondCoef\,TPS lower throughput on the
access-control-enabled path at mean concurrency (95\% CI
[\ThrCondCoefCILow, \ThrCondCoefCIHigh]\,TPS, $p\ThrCondP$). The
condition-by-concurrency interaction, \ThrInteractCoef\,TPS per client, is
not detectable (95\% CI [\ThrInteractCILow, \ThrInteractCIHigh]\,TPS per
client, $p=\ThrInteractP$), and there is no within-level position effect
either ($p=\ThrPositionP$, model $R^2=\ThrFactorialRSq$). The model does
not test for a trend across the session's fixed level order, since the
design cannot separate that from the concurrency effect itself. Averaged
across the ten tested concurrency levels this is a \OverheadMeanPct\%
reduction (SD \OverheadSDPct{} points, range
\OverheadMinPct--\OverheadMaxPct\%; full per-level table, Supplement
Table~S6). A nonsignificant interaction is not proof that the relative
difference stays constant outside the tested range. It means only that no
condition-by-concurrency interaction was detected within the precision of
this experiment, across ten closed-loop concurrency levels from 10 to 100
clients. Across the measured levels, the mean difference is a
workload-specific planning estimate, not a transferable capacity factor.

Both configurations also reached their highest observed throughput at the
same tested concurrency, \PeakBaselineTPS\,TPS for the baseline and
\PeakHrbacTPS\,TPS for HRBAC at \KneeClients{} clients, after which both
decline, HRBAC by \PostKneeDeclinePct\% out to 100 clients. This is the
highest measured throughput under the tested closed-loop workload, not an
independently established capacity ceiling; concurrency was sampled in
steps of ten, so the true peak could sit anywhere in the adjacent
interval, and the shared tested peak does not by itself identify which
resource saturates (Scope~S3, Section~\ref{sec:discussion}) ;
ordering queueing is one candidate, reported for Fabric on x86 by
Thakkar et al.~\cite{thakkar2018performance}, but so are CouchDB service
times, validation and commit capacity, endorsement queueing and gateway
networking, and these clients are also closed-loop, so offered
concurrency is a client count rather than a controlled arrival rate. The
decline past the observed peak is consistent with queueing beyond the
tested workload range, but the trace does not identify the responsible
resource. Admission control or added capacity are therefore engineering
options to test, not conclusions established by this experiment.

\subsection{Peer-multiplicity experiment}
\label{subsec:scaling}

Endorsing peers are normally added to raise physical capacity. Here we
increase configured logical peer multiplicity on four fixed physical
hosts (Supplement Table~S3) and observe write latency, not capacity,
respond. Figure~\ref{fig:scaling} reports write latency as configured peer
count increases from \ScaleMinPeers{} to \ScaleMaxPeers{} at fixed offered
concurrency, across \PartRunsPerConfig{} run-level observations per
configuration executed in counterbalanced order (Supplement Table~S8); the
full latency table is Supplement Table~S7.

\begin{widefig}
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}
\begin{axis}[paperplot,
  width=\linewidth, height=4.8cm,
  xlabel={Endorsing peers}, ylabel={Write latency (ms)},
  xmode=log, log basis x=2, xtick={4,8,16,32}, xticklabels={4,8,16,32},
  xmin=3, xmax=42, ymin=700, ymax=1400,
  colormap/viridis,
  legend pos=north east]
\addplot+[scatter, only marks, mark=*, mark size=1pt, opacity=0.5,
  point meta=explicit, forget plot]
  table[x=x, y=y, meta=block] {figdata/scaling_runs.dat};
\addplot+[mark=*, mark size=1.7pt, blue!65!black, thick,
  error bars/.cd, y dir=both, y explicit]
  table[x=peers, y=mean, y error=sd] {figdata/scaling.dat};
\addlegendentry{Group mean, 95\% CI}
\addplot+[mark=triangle*, mark size=2.1pt, orange!80!black]
  table[x=peers, y=p95] {figdata/scaling.dat};
\addlegendentry{P95}
\end{axis}
\end{tikzpicture}
\caption{Run-level write latency and 95\% confidence intervals by configured logical peer count.}
\label{fig:scaling}
\end{widefig}

Mean write latency falls from \ScaleMinPeerMean\,ms to \ScaleMaxPeerMean\,ms
(run-level means, \PartRunsPerConfig{} runs each), a reduction of
\ScaleLatencyDropPct\% (mean difference \ScaleDiffMs\,ms, 95\% CI
[\ScaleDiffCILow, \ScaleDiffCIHigh]\,ms), and P95 from
\ScaleMinPeerPNinetyFive\,ms to \ScaleMaxPeerPNinetyFive\,ms. We report the
mean difference and its interval as the primary estimate; the Welch $t$
and Cohen's $d$ for the same comparison are large for a mechanical reason
(the between-run standard deviation at fixed peer count is small relative
to a genuinely large peer-count effect, not transaction-level
pseudo-replication: every value entering this comparison is already a
run-level mean), so we report them alongside all 32 individual run-level
means in Supplement Table~S7 rather than in this paragraph. The decline is
close to
log-linear at \ScaleSlope\,ms per doubling with $R^2 = \ScaleRSquared$
across the four configuration means; the same effect, estimated jointly
with run order on all 32 individual runs (Section~\ref{subsec:stats}),
remains significant at $p\OrderEffectTotalPeerP$ while run order does not
($p=\OrderEffectTotalP$). The raw trace does not record reset completion,
so residual carry-over remains within the study scope. This campaign
measured latency only, not
throughput, as a function of peer count (Scope~S2,
Section~\ref{sec:discussion}); the separate, interleaved
concurrency-throughput comparison of Section~\ref{subsec:throughput} used
a fixed peer configuration and is not informative about peer-count
effects.

One hypothesis is that greater logical endorser multiplicity changed
proposal routing or queueing: at four peers each zone has one endorser and
concurrent requests from that zone would serialise behind it, while at 32
peers each zone has eight. Peer queue depth, proposal allocation, CPU
utilisation and state-database service time were not recorded, so the
experiment does not identify the mechanism behind the association. And
every configured peer count above four is hosted on the same four physical
machines as the four-peer configuration, so the comparison varies logical
endorser multiplicity, not genuine physical distribution (S2). For
irrigation control with a two-second
responsiveness budget \cite{leacox2013wireless}, greater logical peer
multiplicity was associated with a larger observed margin against that
threshold in this configuration; whether this association persists under
other workloads, physical deployments or peer topologies remains
untested.

\subsection{Revocation over a multi-week window}
\label{subsec:revocation}

Revocation is where short-duration benchmark measurements are least
informative, because the mechanism fires rarely and its failure mode is
delay rather than error.
Over the deployment, \RevEvents{} lifecycle \emph{stage records} were
logged across \RevDays{} days; these are stage observations rather than
independent revocations, and Section~\ref{subsec:pm_revocation} explains
why end-to-end exposure cannot be recovered from them. On the happy path
the pipeline is quick: CRL publication completes in \RevPubMean\,s on
average (SD \RevPubSD, maximum \RevPubMax), and gossip to all peers takes
\RevGossipMean\,min (SD \RevGossipSD, P95 \RevGossipPNinetyFive, maximum
\RevGossipMax), a tight unimodal propagation distribution with no heavy
tail (Supplement, Table~S9 and Figure~S4).

The longitudinal view is less comfortable. \RevDelayed{} of the
\RevEvents{} stage records, \RevDelayedPct\%, completed in a delayed
state; we give the proportion without a confidence interval, since
correlated stages of the same episode are not independent trials, and CRL
publication is the weakest stage at \RevWorstTypePct\% delayed against
\RevBestTypePct\% for gossip completion. Delayed stages are not slower on
the metrics we can observe, since our timers start when publication or
gossip begins and any interval spent waiting for a gateway to return is
outside the measurement; taken with the connectivity outages of
Section~\ref{subsec:availability}, the pattern points to scheduling and
reachability rather than propagation degrading under load, though
confirming it needs end-to-end timing the trace lacks (Scope~S5,
Section~\ref{sec:discussion}).

The trace contains \RevDenialsOperational{} operational access attempts
recorded as denied for revocation, \RevDenialsPerDay{} per day, spread out
rather than concentrated in any single incident, plus a further
\RevDenialsCampaign{} in the scripted campaign of
Section~\ref{subsec:security}, kept separate since one is field
observation and the other scripted testing. Because the deployment did
not collect the denominator of all post-revocation access attempts, these
counts do not estimate the probability that a revoked credential is
successfully blocked; we report them as evidence enforcement fired
repeatedly in the field, not as a success rate. Nor can the stage records
determine, for any given delayed episode, whether disconnection was the
cause, quantify end-to-end exposure from request to universal enforcement,
or rule out the propagation protocol itself as a contributor: only the
association with the connectivity outages of
Section~\ref{subsec:availability} is available, not a per-episode cause.
For a connected gateway, the design (Supplement, Algorithm~S3) intends
revocation staleness to be bounded by gossip propagation and cache
invalidation, a few minutes; for an unreachable gateway, the scheduled
CRL refresh interval permits a theoretical delay of up to 24 hours. The
stage-level trace cannot determine how often complete revocation
episodes followed either branch, or measure the resulting end-to-end
exposure: only that \RevDelayedPct\% of individual stage records
carried the deployment's delayed label: so we treat the unresolved
upper bound itself, not a measured exposure rate, as the principal
operational weakness the present design leaves open.

\subsection{Authorization boundary enforcement}
\label{subsec:security}

The security evaluation targets the property the system exists to provide,
that no principal acts outside its role, zone or validity window.
\SecAttempts{} scripted attempts ran, each crossing one specific boundary of
the model in Section~\ref{sec:design}, organised at collection time into
\SecScenarios{} named scenarios of \SecPerScenario{} attempts. We do not
report the results by those scenario names, since repetitions of a
scripted request are not independent draws from a population of attacks
(no interval is attached to the block rate), and, more seriously, the
scenario labels do not describe the operations recorded against them; the
full breakdown groups every attempt by the denial mechanism actually
recorded instead (Supplement, Table~S11).

All \SecAttempts{} attempts were refused, invoking \SecDistinctReasons{}
distinct denial mechanisms rather than concentrating in one check, each
spanning every role and zone in the deployment: a suite in which every
attempt is caught by the same check would demonstrate one working
mechanism, not a working model. So the campaign is evidence that the
deployed policy denied what it was asked to deny; it is not a
scenario-by-scenario conformance result, and, combined with
Section~\ref{subsec:pm_policy}, it is not evidence about the intended
design either. A further scope boundary applies regardless of labelling: the
expected-permission oracle against which each attempt is scored is itself
derived from \texttt{roles.go}, so a defect shared between the
implementation and the oracle, such as the inherited audit access of
Section~\ref{subsec:pm_policy}, would not appear as a failure here ; the
campaign shows that the tested requests activated \SecDistinctReasons{}
recorded denial mechanisms in the deployed implementation; because
expected outcomes were derived from that same \texttt{roles.go}, it does
not independently establish consistency with the intended policy,
completeness of enforcement, or correctness for untested requests
(Scope~S4, Section~\ref{sec:discussion}). We additionally cross-check
the full \SecAttempts{}-attempt corpus against
\texttt{chaincode/policy-requirements.json}: the same independent,
requirements-derived oracle built for the role hierarchy
(Section~\ref{subsec:pm_policy}). On the one dimension a static
role/operation matrix can speak to: whether the attacking role holds the
requested operation as a permission at all. \SecOracleInScope{} of
\SecAttempts{} attempts carry a denial reason that makes this claim
(\texttt{ROLE\_INSUFFICIENT} or \texttt{OP\_NOT\_PERMITTED}); the
remainder test zone, certificate, replay or intrusion-detection logic the
role/operation matrix has no opinion on. Of those \SecOracleInScope{},
\SecOracleConsistent{} (\SecOracleConsistentPct\%) are confirmed: the
independent oracle agrees the attacking role lacks that permission.
\SecOracleDiscrepant{} (\SecOracleDiscrepantPct\%) are not: all six
recorded (role, operation) pairs among them: Sensor and Gateway
attempting \texttt{WriteSensor}, Farmer and Gateway attempting
\texttt{ControlZone}, Certifier attempting \texttt{ReadAudit}: are
pairs the independent oracle says the role \emph{should} hold, so the
recorded reason cannot be a pure role/operation question; the corpus does
not carry a separate zone- or resource-ownership attribute that would let
us confirm the alternative (a same-permission, wrong-zone or
wrong-resource request), so we report the discrepancy rather than resolve
it. This extends the independent-oracle check from the role hierarchy
alone to the full boundary-attempt corpus's role/operation dimension; it
remains scored against \texttt{roles.go} directly for the zone, temporal,
replay and identity dimensions the corpus does not separately encode, and
the corpus contains no permitted (positive) requests, only denials, so no
false-denial rate can be estimated from it either. S4 is narrowed
further but not closed. Transport-level attacks,
physical tampering and side-channel extraction are not exercised; mutual
TLS and constant-time primitives address them architecturally, not
empirically.

\subsection{Transmission energy and cryptographic cost}
\label{subsec:integrity}

Reliability of the residue transport is withdrawn (Section~\ref{subsec:pm_crt});
what the campaign measures is cost. Per-event transmission energy falls
\EnergyReductionPct\% [\EnergyReductionCILow, \EnergyReductionCIHigh] from
\EnergySingle\,mJ in single-channel mode to \EnergyCRT\,mJ with residue
encoding, and the signing pipeline (\SignTotal\,\textmu{}s) is negligible
against the \DutyCycleMinutes-minute duty cycle; the full breakdown, and
the qualifications that bound what the energy figure describes (instrumented
payload size, single-node sampling, and the small share of daily energy
transmission represents), are in the supplementary material.

\subsection{Availability}
\label{subsec:availability}

The online decision path, defined as reachable for \emph{all} zones, was
available \UptimePct\% of the deployment across \OutageCount{}
single-gateway connectivity outages (\OutageHoursMin--\OutageHoursMax\,h,
\OutageHoursTotal\,h total: a LoRa link failure, a power fluctuation and a
firmware watchdog reset). The log identifies one affected gateway per event;
it does not independently establish sensor-level continuity for the affected
or unaffected zones. Crediting gateway-hours instead of charging the whole
system for one gateway's outage gives \UptimeGatewayHoursPct\%. Neither
figure is a statement about request success rates, which we did not
record per request. The sensor table contains exactly \WritesPerDay{} rows
per day, but it has only one timestamp and no capture, gateway-receive,
commit, retry or buffer-source field. It therefore cannot establish whether
an outage-period row was captured before disconnection, buffered and replayed,
or reconstructed during processing. The outage log's buffering notes and the
regular row count are consistent with eventual replay, but they do not prove
zero sensor-data loss or uninterrupted service; we report availability and
ledger-row completeness separately.

\FloatBarrier
%%============================================================================
\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}
\label{sec:audit}
%%============================================================================

The implementation audit compared the released code with its specification
and identified four defects and one observability gap that the performance
benchmarks did not expose. The historical implementation remains unchanged
for reproducibility. Separate corrected packages address the policy,
residue, signature and on-ledger revocation defects and add a revocation
correlation identifier; their live-network performance has not been tested.

\subsection{Authorization-policy findings}
\label{subsec:pm_policy}

The role hierarchy in \texttt{roles.go} places Certifier on the human
inheritance chain rather than beside it, so Agronomist and Farmer receive
\texttt{ReadAudit} through inheritance (Equation~\eqref{eq:human},
Table~\ref{tab:permdiff}), and Certifier itself holds \texttt{ReadZone}, so
an auditor could read zone sensor data directly: the separation the
introduction motivates was never in force for any of the \DeployDays{}
days. A separate direct-permission defect grants Agronomist
\texttt{ControlZone} directly, inconsistent with the ``no actuation
rights'' description in Section~\ref{sec:intro}.

We have not patched \texttt{chaincode/hrbac/roles.go}, since doing so
would make the code that produced every measurement here diverge from
what is released as having produced it. Instead,
\texttt{chaincode/hrbac-corrected/} fixes both. Certifier is removed from
Agronomist's and Farmer's ancestor sets, and \texttt{ReadZone} moves to
their direct grants. \texttt{ControlZone} is removed from Agronomist's
direct grant; Farmer no longer inherits it from Agronomist, so Farmer
receives its own direct grant instead. Every other effective permission is
unchanged. Three regression tests verify this.
\texttt{TestAuditorSeparationHolds} and
\texttt{TestAgronomistCannotControlZone} each fail against
\texttt{chaincode/hrbac}'s hierarchy and pass against the corrected one,
confirmed with a throwaway copy run against the deployed package.
\texttt{TestMatchesRequirementsOracle} checks the corrected hierarchy cell
by cell, across all seven roles and ten permissions, against
\texttt{chaincode/policy-requirements.json}, a matrix authored from the
manuscript's stakeholder requirements independently of either
\texttt{roles.go}, and fails and passes the same way: the independent-oracle
check required by Section~\ref{subsec:security} (S4,
Section~\ref{sec:discussion}). The correction is a policy patch, not a
performance re-run (S5); Section~\ref{subsec:security} confirms only that
the tested requests activated the \emph{deployed} implementation's own
recorded denial mechanisms, not that it validates the intended design.

A Go benchmark compares \texttt{CheckAccess} in the deployed and corrected
packages using the same in-memory mock state, workload and hardware. It
executes one grant and one denial 2\,000 times in each of five runs
(\texttt{go test -bench=CheckAccess -benchtime=2000x -count=5}); raw output
is provided in \texttt{CHAINCODE\_MICROBENCHMARK.md}. Grant-path
execution averages 282.9\,\textmu{}s (SD 11.8) for \texttt{chaincode/hrbac}
against 276.9\,\textmu{}s (SD 4.9) for \texttt{chaincode/hrbac-corrected}
(Welch $t=1.06$, $p=0.33$); deny-path execution averages 277.3\,\textmu{}s
(SD 5.8) against 281.9\,\textmu{}s (SD 3.8) ($t=-1.48$, $p=0.18$).
Neither comparison detected a difference at this sample size, and neither
establishes equivalence. These mock-stub execution times exclude endorsement,
ordering, commitment and network delay, so they do not bound performance
differences in a live Fabric deployment (S5).

\subsection{Residue-recovery findings}
\label{subsec:pm_crt}

As Section~\ref{subsec:firmware} sets out, recovery from an arbitrary pair
of residues is unique only below the smallest pairwise product of the
moduli. The deployed firmware used $\{97, 101, 103\}$, so the recovery
bound depends on which residue is missing, as Table~\ref{tab:crtpairs}
shows. The trace does not identify the missing residue, so a per-pair count
is unavailable.

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{Pairwise recovery bounds for the deployed residue moduli.}
\label{tab:crtpairs}
\small
\begin{tabularx}{\columnwidth}{@{}lX@{}}
\toprule
Residues present (missing modulus) & Recovery bound \\
\midrule
97, 101 (missing 103) & $97\times 101 = 9\,797$ \\
97, 103 (missing 101) & $97\times 103 = 9\,991$ \\
101, 103 (missing 97) & $101\times 103 = 10\,403$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{table} We reconstructed the packed
value for all \CRTExceedN{} committed readings from the released
engineering-unit columns using the exact encoding in
\texttt{esp32/main/main.c}: the trace's minimum is \CRTPackedMin{} and
maximum \CRTPackedMax{}, so \CRTExceedCount{} of \CRTExceedN{}
(\CRTExceedPct\%) exceed the smallest bound. \CRTRecovered{} readings
(\CRTLossRatePct\%) arrived with two of three residues; since every
packed value here exceeded even the largest bound, each such
reconstruction deterministically returned the value reduced modulo its
pair's bound rather than the original, regardless of which residue was
missing. All \CRTRecovered{} two-residue reconstructions are therefore
mathematically incorrect, and the original cannot be recovered after the
fact, since raw residue packets were not retained.

The corrected firmware's $\{253, 254, 255\}$ moduli (bound $64\,262$) are
checked by exhaustive enumeration too: every legal input to the corrected
8-bit soil encoding gives a maximum packed value of $51\,455$
($255 \times 201 + 200$, the full legal domain), below the bound, so
every value the corrected encoder can produce is uniquely recoverable.
Quantising soil moisture from twelve to eight bits to reach that bound
introduces a maximum quantisation error of \QuantErrMaxPct\% of full
scale (RMS \QuantErrRMSPct\%). Whether this satisfies a particular
agricultural application depends on its measurement-accuracy requirement;
no manufacturer tolerance claim is inferred here.

\subsection{Signature-verification findings}
\label{subsec:pm_signature}

The defect above would have been caught downstream had the signature path
been correct; it was not. The firmware signs SHA-256 over a packed binary
struct holding device identifier, reading identifier, raw soil moisture,
temperature and timestamp, but the gateway verified an Ed25519 signature
over an ASCII rendering built from the \emph{decoded} value, a different
message, so verification could not succeed against a genuine sensor
signature; the same routine also returned success whenever a signature
was absent, a fail-open default intended to let the gateway run without
production credentials. Taken together, the \SigValidPct\%
signature-validity figure in the trace cannot mean that sensor signatures
were checked and passed, and we withdraw the integrity claim rather than
qualify it.

The firmware signs the 32-byte SHA-256 digest of the packed struct with
Ed25519 rather than using standard Ed25519ph, which uses SHA-512.
The corrected verifier SHA-256-hashes the reconstructed bytes
before checking the signature, matching \texttt{esp32/main/signing.c}
exactly, and the test suite includes a fixed, published byte-for-byte
vector an independent reimplementation can check against without running
this codebase (Supplement, ``Signature test vector''). This is a
legacy-compatible corrected verifier, not a migration to standard
Ed25519 or Ed25519ph semantics: the deployed firmware's prehash
construction cannot be changed without reflashing physical sensor nodes
this study does not have further access to, so the correction matches
what that firmware actually signs rather than replacing it with a
scheme-versioned protocol.

\subsection{Certificate-revocation enforcement gap}
\label{subsec:pm_crl}

A fourth defect surfaced during a subsequent implementation audit. \texttt{CheckAccess} reads a \texttt{crl:}-prefixed world
state key to decide whether a caller's certificate has been revoked
(Section~\ref{subsec:zones}), but no transaction in the deployed chaincode
ever wrote such a key. The operational revocation workflow
(\texttt{scripts/generate-crl.sh}) already tried to call an
\texttt{UpdateCRL} transaction as part of every revocation, but the
deployed package has no function by that name: the call failed with an
unknown-transaction error every time, the script logged the failure and
moved on, and the on-ledger certificate-revocation branch of the decision
algorithm was dead code for the full \DeployDays{} days. The missing transaction did not remove the separate role-deletion mechanism. The deployment also relied on the certificate authority's revocation list at the mutual-TLS layer; however, the available trace does not independently reconstruct distribution, reload and enforcement of that list across every component. The defensible historical evidence is therefore the recorded role deletion, not complete end-to-end certificate-revocation enforcement. None of the reported performance or
security numbers depend on the missing transaction, because nothing in the
deployed workflow ever exercised it.

\texttt{chaincode/hrbac-corrected} adds \texttt{UpdateCRL}: it parses a
certificate revocation list in the format
\texttt{scripts/generate-crl.sh} already produces, writes the
corresponding \texttt{crl:}-prefixed state entries, and is gated to the
Admin role like the package's other administrative transactions.
\texttt{TestUpdateCRLWrites\-RevocationEntries\-AndDeniesCheckAccess} and
\texttt{TestUpdateCRLRequiresAdmin} in that package's test suite are the
regression tests. This implements the missing on-ledger update path for future testing; it cannot
retroactively enforce a check the historical trace shows was never
enforced.

\subsection{Revocation observability}
\label{subsec:pm_revocation}

The revocation trace records lifecycle stages with no key linking them
into episodes: of \RevSubjects{} subjects, \RevComplete{} carry all four
stages and \RevSingleStage{} appear once. End-to-end exposure, the
interval from revocation request to enforcement everywhere, is the
quantity an operator needs, and the historical trace cannot reconstruct it
(S5).

The corrected implementation adds the correlation identifier required to address this gap. \texttt{RevokeRole} and
\texttt{UpdateCRL} in \texttt{chaincode/hrbac-corrected} both stamp an
\texttt{EpisodeID} field on their audit entries, taken from the same nonce
value \texttt{scripts/revoke-cert.sh} and \texttt{scripts/generate-crl.sh}
now share for one revocation request. On the gateway side,
\texttt{PolicyCache.invalidate}/\texttt{invalidate\_all} log that same
token when a cache is cleared, and a new \texttt{Gateway.handle\_revocation}
method gives an event-driven listener a real, tested place to call. Before
this change, nothing in the repository ever called
\texttt{PolicyCache.invalidate}, so the event-driven invalidation this
article describes had no caller anywhere in this codebase; a live
deployment's gossip or chaincode-event subscription would still need to be
wired to that method, which is outside what the corrected implementation changes. What
this gives a future deployment is a real, joinable key across the
chaincode and gateway sides of one revocation. It does not, and cannot,
resolve episodes already present in the historical trace analysed here:
that data was collected before the correlation identifier existed.

\subsection{Cross-layer implications}
\label{subsec:pm_pattern}

The defects occurred at interfaces between components: a role hierarchy
disagreeing with its own description, a transport whose recovery bound the
encoder never checked, a signature verified over the wrong bytes, and a
ledger check with no writer. The artifact now generates the permission
table from \texttt{roles.go} instead of transcribing it, checks every legal
encoder input against the recovery bound, tests gateway verification
against the firmware's byte layout, and tests that \texttt{UpdateCRL}
actually denies a caller whose certificate it revokes.

Table~\ref{tab:datavalidity} states, for each finding, what a reader may
still treat as valid and what they may not.

\begin{table}[pos=t]
\caption{Validity and permitted interpretation of evidence affected by the implementation audit.}
\label{tab:datavalidity}
\small
