\subsection{Performance implications}
\label{subsec:implications}

Four consequences follow, each contradicting a plausible default
assumption.

The recorded authorization-associated span accounted for roughly a quarter
of the write path, and it varied less across tested peer configurations
than the uninstrumented remainder did. It sits at \PartAccessPct\% of the
write path at \ScaleMinPeers{} peers and does not move appreciably as
configured peer count scales, so optimising policy evaluation is bounded
above by roughly a quarter of write latency (Scope~S1). Because
expired-role cleanup mutates state inside \texttt{CheckAccess}, read-intent
checks are endorsed rather than served as peer queries. A read-only
decision path, with expiry reclaimed by a background sweep instead, would
take reads off the consensus path, at the cost of the durable ordered audit
transaction a committed \texttt{CheckAccess} currently produces, and it
would need revocation freshness maintained another way. We call that a
high-value candidate worth the trade-off in most deployments, not an
unconditional recommendation.

Peers are associated with lower tail latency here; treat throughput
separately. Configured logical peer multiplicity is associated with a
close-to-log-linear reduction in write latency (Section~\ref{subsec:scaling}),
supported by a joint regression on peer count and run order once the
earlier order confound is designed out (S2). The separate, interleaved
concurrency experiment, meanwhile, found the same observed throughput peak
for both arms without locating the saturating resource (S3). The phrase
``peers buy latency, not capacity'' describes only the latency side, and a
deployment weighing more endorsers against more capacity should measure
both under its own workload.

Budget the access-control-enabled path empirically, not as a universal
constant. Across the tested closed-loop concurrency levels, the complete
access-control-enabled path averaged \OverheadMeanPct\% lower throughput
than the comparison path, and no condition-by-concurrency interaction was
detected. That supports using roughly that figure as a workload-specific
planning estimate for the tested peer count and workload, but it does not
establish a fixed derating factor that transfers to other peer counts,
workloads or high-load regimes.

Revocation is the weak link. It is the only mechanism whose behaviour
materially degraded over the deployment: \RevDelayed{} of \RevEvents{}
stage records carry the deployment's delayed label. Their association with
recorded connectivity outages motivates a reachability hypothesis, but the
trace cannot determine per-episode cause or exclude the propagation
protocol as a contributor (S5). Event-driven credential status checking
\cite{w3c_vc_status_list} and constrained-device status protocols such as
TinyOCSP \cite{fedrecheski2023tinyocsp} remove the dependency on a
scheduled publication reaching a possibly-disconnected gateway, whichever
the cause turns out to be; the corrected implementation's episode-correlation identifier
(Section~\ref{subsec:pm_revocation}) is a smaller step in the same
direction, aimed at measuring the problem rather than fixing it outright.

Direct numerical comparison against prior systems is limited because
hardware, workload, transaction semantics and latency definitions differ
(Supplement, Table~S1), a point
Abang et al.~\cite{abang2024latency} make about the Fabric latency
literature generally; the comparison we regard as meaningful is the
internal one, the same network, hardware and workload with and without
the access-control layer (Section~\ref{subsec:throughput}), since it is
reproducible from the released artifact.

\subsection{Scope and validity}
\label{subsec:notvalidated}
\label{subsec:limits}
\label{subsec:threats}

The threat model treats orderers and the certificate authority as
non-malicious under crash-fault-tolerant Raft, and physical tampering and
side-channel extraction as residual risk, architecturally addressed by
mutual TLS and constant-time primitives rather than empirically tested.
Within that scope, three things this deployment measured are not the same
as validating the intended design. Section~\ref{subsec:security} measures
refusals against the \emph{deployed} policy, which
Section~\ref{subsec:pm_policy} shows is not the intended one, and its
oracle is derived from the same code it tests (S4), so it is conformance
testing of one implementation, not a security proof, and says nothing
about an adversary who deviates from the scripted campaign. The
audit's corrections are patches to code, not to the archived timing
measurements. A chaincode-only microbenchmark (Section~\ref{subsec:pm_policy})
did not detect a statistically significant difference in \texttt{CheckAccess} execution cost between the deployed and corrected role hierarchies, but that isolates Go
execution time inside the mockStub harness used to test both packages; it
says nothing about whether the corrected chaincode preserves the write
latency, throughput and recorded span this article reports for a real
Fabric network, which has not been re-run (S5). And overhead throughout is
attributed by differencing against a
baseline with the access-control chaincode removed, which also removes the
audit write and the nonce check, so every reported cost bounds the
access-control \emph{layer} rather than an isolated permission decision.
Table~\ref{tab:datavalidity} in Section~\ref{sec:audit} states, trace
by trace, what remains usable after the audit.

Table~\ref{tab:canonlimits} defines the evidence boundaries and the
measurements needed to extend the study scope.

\begin{widetab}[pos=t]
\caption{Evidence boundaries and measurements required to extend the study scope.}
\label{tab:canonlimits}
\footnotesize
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}p{0.05\linewidth}Xp{0.38\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
& Scope boundary & Extension required \\
\midrule
S1 & Timer boundaries and policy-path labels are incomplete. &
     Timestamp Fabric stages and vary hierarchy depth and denial reason. \\
S2 & Logical peers were tested on four hosts in one campaign; peer-count throughput was not measured. &
     Repeat across physical hosts and seasons, measuring latency and throughput. \\
S3 & One ascending-concurrency session cannot identify capacity or the limiting resource. &
     Randomise sessions and record queues, block fill and database service time. \\
S4 & The denial-only corpus cannot estimate false denials or validate every policy dimension independently. &
     Add permitted requests, zone and ownership fields, mutation tests and an external oracle. \\
S5 & Historical stages lack episode keys, and corrected live-network performance is unmeasured. &
     Populate the new episode key and repeat network benchmarks with corrected code. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{widetab}

One deployment, one season, one site, and a workload dominated by a
regular sensor-write stream: we regard the recorded span's small, stable
share of the write path as more transferable than the millisecond values
(S2). The topology trace's coordinate columns are unreliable and unused,
and a multi-device energy campaign over the full authenticated frame would
generalise Section~\ref{subsec:integrity}'s single-node figure.

\FloatBarrier
%%============================================================================
\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}
%%============================================================================

This study evaluated blockchain access control during a \DeployDays-day
agricultural edge-IoT deployment and two controlled campaigns. The recorded
authorization-associated span averaged \PartAccess\,ms within a
\PartTotal\,ms write path. Increasing configured logical peers from
\ScaleMinPeers{} to \ScaleMaxPeers{} on four fixed hosts reduced the
uninstrumented remainder by \PartEndorser\,ms. The interleaved throughput
experiment found that the access-control-enabled path averaged
\OverheadMeanPct\% lower throughput across the tested range. These findings
apply to the evaluated topology and workload.

The implementation audit identified policy, residue-recovery,
signature-verification and certificate-revocation defects, together with a
revocation-observability gap the corrected implementation partly closes in code with a
shared correlation identifier. The released corrections preserve the
historical implementation for reproducibility. A chaincode-only
microbenchmark finds no measurable decision-cost difference between the
deployed and corrected role hierarchies, but network-level performance
under the corrected chaincode has not been re-benchmarked. The public
artifact provides the traces, schedules, code, tests, and analysis needed
to reproduce the results and evaluate the design in other settings.

\section*{Ethics and data protection}

The traces record authorization decisions whose subjects include farm
operators and administrators, so caller identifiers are potentially personal
data. Oversight for the deployment was provided by the University of Buea
Faculty of Engineering and Technology's departmental research ethics review,
which issued a non-interventional technical study determination
(reference FET-CE-2025-014, 14~July~2025) covering the collection of
operational, performance and access-control traces from consenting farm
personnel; no biomedical or behavioural data were in scope. Each
participating operator and administrator gave written informed consent before
the deployment began,
covering data collection, the use of pseudonymised traces in this article and
their public release; participation was voluntary and could be withdrawn
without affecting farm operations. Identifiers in the released dataset are
pseudonyms assigned at collection (\texttt{usr-} and \texttt{sns-} prefixes);
no names, contact details or free-text fields were collected, and the
mapping from pseudonym to individual was destroyed by the data-collection
team before the dataset was prepared for release, so no reverse mapping
exists for us or for a reader to reconstruct. The site is identified at
settlement granularity rather than by field coordinates, and the coordinate
columns in the topology trace are unreliable in any case
(Section~\ref{subsec:threats}). No sensor data revealing an individual's
conduct beyond routine farm operation was collected. These are the grounds
on which the pseudonymised operational traces are released alongside this
article.
